analysis.one_liner: Lets the Energy Secretary cap wholesale electricity prices across the West when regulators fail to act.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 32 cosponsors from both parties, was referred to a House subcommittee in February 2001 and never received a markup or vote, dying when the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: During the Western electricity crisis, wholesale power prices in Western states spiked far beyond the cost of producing electricity, and the federal regulator in charge, FERC, was not imposing region-wide price limits. This bill would have let the Secretary of Energy step in and impose an interim cap on wholesale electricity prices across the Western region whenever prices were found unjust, unreasonable, or far above production cost and FERC had failed to act. Any state's governor could have opted out of the cap.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and businesses in Western states — above all California, which was experiencing blackouts and soaring bills at the time — would pay capped wholesale electricity prices based on producers' actual costs plus a fair return, rather than uncontrolled market prices.

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the Secretary of Energy to impose an interim regional price limitation, or a cost-of-service based rate, on wholesale sales of electricity whenever FERC finds the rate unjust, unreasonable, or unduly preferential and the Secretary finds the price threatens public health, safety, or a state or regional economy and FERC has failed to fix it.

The limitation is defined as a region-wide wholesale price cap covering the Western Systems Coordinating Council region, with limits differentiated by season, time of day, and usage patterns rather than a flat cap.

A capped rate would be based on producers' actual fixed and variable costs plus a return on invested capital, and would remain in effect until the Secretary determines the market reflects just and reasonable rates.

analysis.who_pays: Wholesale electricity generators and power marketers selling into Western markets, whose prices would be limited to cost-of-service levels when the cap applies, instead of whatever the crisis-driven market would bear.

drawbacks.text: A cap tied to cost of service or marginal cost can reduce the financial incentive to build new power plants, which critics argue can worsen supply shortages over time — a serious concern during a crisis caused in part by tight supply.

The bill concentrates sweeping discretion in the Energy Secretary, who could override rates within FERC's jurisdiction whenever the Secretary judged prices 'significantly' above marginal cost and threatening the economy — a vague standard that could make electricity pricing politically driven rather than regulatorily consistent.

The governor of any state in the region could waive the cap, which could produce a patchwork of limits across neighboring states and complicate the regional electricity market the cap was meant to calm.
The cap would apply only to contracts entered into or renewed after enactment, so existing high-priced contracts would remain in place.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers caught in the 2000-01 Western price spike, the benefit of cost-based wholesale prices was large and immediate. The drawbacks — dampened investment in new generation and a large transfer of rate-setting power to a cabinet secretary on loose standards — are real, but the bill was designed as an interim emergency tool, not a permanent price control, and states could opt out. A stronger design might have set clearer triggers and a firm sunset.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, passed along to its Energy and Air Quality subcommittee within three weeks, and was never brought up again before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Duncan Hunter of California introduced the bill on January 20, 2001, during the peak of California's electricity crisis.
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
On February 7, 2001, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality, where it remained with no markup, no vote, and no further action.
The bill attracted 32 cosponsors — 29 of 208 House Democrats and 3 of 223 House Republicans.
The 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, and the bill died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wholesale electricity generators and power marketers stayed better off: without the bill, they continued selling into Western markets at uncapped crisis prices, and no precedent was set for the Energy Secretary to override FERC on rates.

for.name: Duncan Hunter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to authorize interim regional caps on wholesale electricity prices.

for.name: California original cosponsors (Eshoo, Cunningham, Issa, Capps, Lee)
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Energy and Air Quality Subcommittee on February 7, 2001, and never scheduled a markup or vote on it.

against.name: Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
against.role: Federal regulator of wholesale electricity markets
against.what_they_did: The bill was written to work around FERC's failure to impose region-wide price limits; FERC resisted broad Western price caps during the 2000-01 crisis before ordering limited caps in mid-2001.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan — 29 of 208 House Democrats and 3 of 223 House Republicans cosponsored, including the Republican sponsor — but the bill never got a vote, so no party split on the merits was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Wholesale electricity generators and power marketers
industries.note: The bill would have capped their wholesale rates at cost-of-service levels whenever prices ran far above production cost and regulators failed to act. During the Western crisis these sellers charged crisis-driven market prices that flowed directly into consumers' electric bills.

industries.industry: Utilities that buy wholesale power (especially in California and the West)
industries.note: Buyers of wholesale power — including California's utilities, which were paying extreme market prices at the time — would have purchased under cost-based caps, easing pressure that could otherwise be passed on to their customers.
